instrument.full_name: Convention on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Certain Conventional Weapons which may be deemed to be Excessively Injurious or to have Indiscriminate Effects
instrument.adopted_at: Geneva, Switzerland (United Nations Conference on Prohibitions or Restrictions of Use of Certain Conventional Weapons)
instrument.key_non_parties: Signatories that have not ratified: Egypt, Nigeria, Sudan and Viet Nam. States that have neither signed nor acceded include Iran, Syria, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Ethiopia and Kenya. All five permanent members of the Security Council, India, Pakistan and Israel are parties (UN Treaty Collection, XXVI-2, as of 11 October 2026).
instrument.duration_clause: The Convention contains no duration clause. It continues for each party until denunciation under Art. 9.
instrument.extension_clause: No extension clause; none is needed because no term is fixed.
instrument.withdrawal_clause: Art. 9: any party may denounce the Convention or any annexed Protocol by notifying the Depositary. Denunciation takes effect one year after receipt, but if the denouncing party is then engaged in an armed conflict or occupation covered by Art. 1, it remains bound until the end of the conflict or occupation and the completion of release and repatriation of protected persons (and, for Protocols covering UN missions, until those functions end). Denunciation of the Convention applies to all annexed Protocols by which the party is bound, and does not affect obligations already incurred for prior acts.
instrument.amendment_clause: Art. 8(1): any party may propose amendments to the Convention or to a Protocol by which it is bound. The Depositary convenes a conference if a majority, not less than eighteen parties, agrees. Amendments are adopted and enter into force in the same manner as the Convention (Art. 5: six months after the twentieth instrument); amendments to the Convention may be adopted only by its parties, and amendments to a Protocol only by parties bound by it. The text does not specify a voting rule; in practice conferences have adopted decisions by consensus. Art. 8(2) provides a parallel procedure for additional protocols on other categories of conventional weapons.
instrument.entry_into_force_requirements: Art. 5(1): six months after deposit of the twentieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession; for later states, six months after their own deposit (Art. 5(2)). Under Art. 4(3), a state must, when it joins, notify its consent to be bound by at least two of the annexed Protocols. Each Protocol enters into force six months after twenty states have consented to it (Art. 5(3)-(4)). The Convention entered into force on 2 December 1983.
instrument.count_basis: English authentic text of the framework Convention (title, preamble and Arts. 1-11), excluding the annexed Protocols, taken from the UN certified true copy (UNTC PDF, pages 25-32) by OCR and counted as whitespace-separated tokens; page numbers removed. Approximate (plus or minus about 1 percent for OCR noise). Operative Arts. 1-11 alone: about 1,955 words.
instrument.weapons_systems_limited: None directly. The framework Convention restricts no weapon itself; it is an umbrella that sets scope, entry into force, review and denunciation rules for annexed Protocols (I-V), which carry the substantive restrictions and are separate records.
instrument.key_provisions: Art. 1 (as concluded): applies to international armed conflicts under Art. 2 common to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and to situations in Art. 1(4) of Additional Protocol I (the 2001 amendment extending scope to non-international conflicts is a separate record). Art. 2: does not detract from other IHL obligations. Arts. 3-5: signature, ratification, entry into force; consent to at least two Protocols required (Art. 4(3)). Art. 6: dissemination of the Convention and Protocols, including in military instruction. Art. 7: treaty relations with non-parties and with authorities under Additional Protocol I Art. 96(3). Art. 8: amendments, additional protocols and review conferences. Art. 9: denunciation with one year's notice. Arts. 10-11: depositary and authentic texts.
instrument.behavior_change: Limited at the framework level. The Convention's only operative conduct obligation is dissemination of its rules to armed forces and the public (Art. 6). Substantive behavioural constraints arise only through the Protocols a party accepts. The 2006 compliance mechanism decision added politically agreed annual national reporting on dissemination, legislation and technical measures.
instrument.historical_background: Work on restricting specific conventional weapons grew out of ICRC expert conferences (Lucerne 1974, Lugano 1976) and the 1974-77 Diplomatic Conference that produced the Additional Protocols, which left weapon-specific rules unresolved. A United Nations conference met in Geneva from 10 to 28 September 1979 and from 15 September to 10 October 1980, and on 10 October 1980 adopted the Convention with Protocols I-III. The Convention was opened for signature in New York on 10 April 1981 and entered into force on 2 December 1983. Its modular design has since allowed new Protocols (IV in 1995, V in 2003) and a scope amendment (2001), and since 2014 it has hosted the international discussions on lethal autonomous weapons systems.

section_provisions_md:
### Nature of the instrument
- The Convention is a framework treaty. It contains no substantive weapons restrictions of its own; those are set out in the annexed Protocols (I-V), which are separate records.
- Any Protocol a party accepts "shall for that Party form an integral part of this Convention" (Art. 4(5)).

### Scope (Arts. 1, 2 and 7)
- As concluded, the Convention and its Protocols apply in international armed conflicts under Art. 2 common to the 1949 Geneva Conventions, including wars of national liberation described in Art. 1(4) of Additional Protocol I (Art. 1). The 2001 amendment extending scope to non-international armed conflicts is a separate record.
- Nothing in the Convention detracts from other obligations under international humanitarian law (Art. 2).
- Parties bound by a Protocol remain bound in their mutual relations even if another party to the conflict is not (Art. 7(1)), and are bound towards a non-party that accepts and applies the Convention or Protocol and notifies the Depositary (Art. 7(2)).
- Art. 7(4) lets an authority of the type in Additional Protocol I Art. 96(3) accept and apply the Convention in a conflict against a party.

### Joining and entry into force (Arts. 3-5)
- Open for signature in New York for twelve months from 10 April 1981; thereafter by accession (Arts. 3-4).
- A joining state must consent to at least two annexed Protocols (Art. 4(3)) and may accept others later (Art. 4(4)).
- Entry into force six months after the twentieth instrument; Protocols separately after twenty consents (Art. 5).

### Conduct obligation
- Dissemination: parties must disseminate the Convention and their accepted Protocols in peace and war and include them in military instruction (Art. 6).

### Review, amendment and additional protocols (Art. 8)
- Amendments to the Convention or a Protocol: a conference is convened if a majority of not less than eighteen parties agrees; amendments enter into force like the Convention (Art. 8(1)).
- Additional protocols on other categories of conventional weapons may be adopted by a conference open to all states (Art. 8(2)).
- If no conference is held within ten years of entry into force, any party may request a review conference (Art. 8(3)). Since 1995 parties have in practice convened review conferences about every five years.

### Denunciation, depositary and texts (Arts. 9-11)
- Denunciation takes effect one year after notice, deferred while the party is engaged in an Art. 1 conflict or occupation; it covers all Protocols the party has accepted (Art. 9).
- The UN Secretary-General is Depositary (Art. 10). Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish texts are equally authentic (Art. 11).

### Later decisions (not treaty text)
- The 2006 Third Review Conference adopted a compliance mechanism: consultation and cooperation on compliance concerns, and national reports on dissemination, legislation, technical measures and cooperation. The 2011 Fourth Review Conference set 31 March as the annual reporting deadline.
- The text contains no verification, inspection, enforcement or dispute-settlement provisions.
section_history_md:
### Origins and negotiation
Weapon-specific restrictions were left unresolved by the 1974-77 Diplomatic Conference that produced the Additional Protocols to the Geneva Conventions, after preparatory ICRC expert conferences at Lucerne (1974) and Lugano (1976). A United Nations conference met in Geneva from 10 to 28 September 1979 and from 15 September to 10 October 1980. On 10 October 1980 it adopted the Convention with Protocols I (non-detectable fragments), II (mines and booby-traps) and III (incendiary weapons).

### Entry into force and participation
The Convention opened for signature in New York on 10 April 1981 and 50 states signed. It entered into force on 2 December 1983 and was registered as UNTS No. 22495 (vol. 1342). As of 11 October 2026 the UN Treaty Collection lists 128 parties. Egypt, Nigeria, Sudan and Viet Nam have signed but not ratified. Trinidad and Tobago (29 July 2024) is the most recent accession.

### Review conferences and development
- First Review Conference (Vienna, 25 September to 13 October 1995; Geneva, January and April-May 1996): adopted Protocol IV on blinding lasers and Amended Protocol II.
- Second Review Conference (Geneva, 11-21 December 2001): amended Art. 1 to cover non-international armed conflicts (in force 18 May 2004) and launched the expert work that produced Protocol V, adopted by the Meeting of States Parties on 28 November 2003.
- Third Review Conference (Geneva, 7-17 November 2006): adopted the compliance mechanism, a universalization plan and a sponsorship programme. An Implementation Support Unit followed in November 2009.
- Fourth Review Conference (Geneva, 14-25 November 2011): did not reach consensus on a draft Protocol VI on cluster munitions.
- Fifth Review Conference (Geneva, 12-16 December 2016): established a Group of Governmental Experts on lethal autonomous weapons systems.
- Sixth Review Conference (Geneva, 13-17 December 2021): considered the continuation of that work.
- The Seventh Review Conference is scheduled for 16-20 November 2026 in Geneva, after a Preparatory Committee on 7-9 September 2026. It had not yet met at the time of coding.

### Compliance and operation
The framework text has no verification or enforcement machinery, and no formal compliance finding has been made under it. Allegations about particular weapons (for example incendiary weapons or mines) concern the Protocols and are recorded there. Operational strain has been financial: the Arms Control Association reported in 2017 that unpaid assessments, most notably by Brazil, forced cancellation of meetings.
